Ἰησοῦ μηδέποτε γενομένους ἐν ἁμαρτίᾳ, οὐδὲν ἧττον κἀκείνους νεκροὺς εἶναι τῇ
ἁμαρτίᾳ, ὥσπερ χωρὶ νόμου ἁμαρτία ἦν νεκρά, οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ ποτὲ ζῇν ἐλθοῦσα ἐπὶ τὸ
γενέσθαι νεκρά. δείκνυσι δὲ ὁ θεῖος ἀπόστολος καὶ ἑτέρωθεν τῆς νίκης τὴν
εὐκολίαν, ἁμαρτία γὰρ ὑμῶν, φησίν, οὐκέτι κυριεύσει, οὐ γάρ ἐστε ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλ'
ὑπὸ χάριν. πρόσχες ἐνταῦθα τῇ ἀποστολικῇ ἀκριβείᾳ, τίνα τρόπον τὸ κυριεύειν
τάσσων ἐπὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος καὶ ἐφ' ἡμῶν ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ σωτῆρος θάνατο εἶπεν αὐτοῦ
οὐκέτι κυριεύ ει, ἐπὶ δὲ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτία γὰρ ὑμῶν οὐ κυριεύσει· οὔτε γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ
σωτῆρος ἔπρεπεν λέγεσθαι τὸ ἁμαρτία αὐτοῦ οὐ κυριεύσει, οὔτε ἐφ' ὑμῶν
κυριώτερον ἦν τὸ θάνατο ὑμῶν οὐ κυριεύ ει· καὶ ἵνα μὴ ταὐτὸν περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος
καὶ ἡμῶν λέγηται ὡς παραπλησίων. μετὰ ταῦτα ὥσπερ αἰτίαν παριστὰς τοῦ
ἁμαρτίαν ἡμῶν μὴ κυριεύειν φησὶ τὸ οὐ γάρ ἐστε ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλ' ὑπὸ χάριν· κατὰ
γὰρ αὐτὸν τὸν Παῦλον ἡ δύναμι τῆ ἁμαρτία ὁ νόμο ἐ τίν, καὶ νόμο παρει ῆλθεν
ἵνα πλεονά ῃ τὸ παράπτωμα ἀλλ' ὅπου ἐπλεόνα εν ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐκεῖ ὑπερεπερί ευ εν ἡ
χάρι · νῦν δὲ ἐσμὲν ὑπὸ τὴν περι εύου αν χάριν, διότι οὐκέτι ἐσμὲν ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλ'
ὑπὸ χάριν. δικαίῳ γὰρ νόμο οὐ κεῖται, οὐ γὰρ δέεται τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ γράμματος νομικῆς
διδασκαλίας εἰς τὸ τηρεῖν τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ θεοῦ θεοδίδακτος ὤν, ὡς Παῦλος
διδάσκει λέγων περὶ δὲ τῆ ἀγάπη οὐ χρείαν ἔχετε ὑμῖν γράφε θαι, ὑμεῖ γὰρ
θεοδίδακτοί ἐ τε εἰ τὸ ἀγαπᾶν ἀλλήλου . εἴ τινι οὖν συμπέφυκεν ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ νόμος,
ὡς μὴ ἕτερον μὲν βούλεσθαι τὸν νόμον ἕτερον δὲ εἶναι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ὁ
τοιοῦτος οὐκ ἐστὶν ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλ' ὑπὸ χάριν· οὕτω νοητέον ἀλλ' ἦν ἐν τῷ νόμῳ
κυρίου τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ. 32 vi 19, 20 ὥσπερ γὰρ παρεστήσατε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν δοῦλα
τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ, καὶ τῇ ἀνομίᾳ εἰς τὴν ἀνομίαν, οὕτως νῦν παραστήσατε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν
δοῦλα τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ εἰς ἁγιασμόν· ὅτε γὰρ δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε
τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ. ἐπειδή, ὡς πολλαχοῦ (φησίν) ἐτηρήσαμεν, τὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὄνομα
ἀντὶ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἔσθ' ὅτε παραλαμβάνεται, λεκτέον ὅτι καὶ νῦν τοιοῦτόν ἐστι τὸ
λεγόμενον ὅτε δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε τῇ ἀρετῇ. καὶ παρ ακολουθεῖ
τῷ γενικῷ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὀνόματι τὸ γενικὸν τῆς ἀρετῆς δικαιοσύνην ἐν τούτοις
ὀνομάζεσθαι. δόξει δὲ εἰδικῶς τὸ εἰς ἁγιασμὸν λέγειν, προτρεπόμενος εἰς ἁγνείαν
καὶ καθαρότητα βίου τὸν δυνάμενον χωρῆ αι. 33 vi 21, 22 τίνα οὖν καρπὸν εἴχετε
τότε ἐφ' οἷς νῦν ἐπαισχύνεσθε; τὸ γὰρ τέλος ἐκείνων θάνατος· νυνὶ δέ,
ἐλευθερωθέντες ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας δουλωθέντες δὲ τῷ θεῷ, ἔχετε τὸν καρπὸν ὑμῶν
εἰς ἁγιασμόν, τὸ δὲ τέλος ζωὴν αἰώνιον. ἐξευτελίζων τὸν καρπὸν τῶν δούλων τῆς
ἁμαρτίας ὡς οὐδενὸς ἄξιον λόγου τοῦτό φησιν· ἐφ' οἷς γάρ τις πρότερον ἐν ἁμαρτίᾳ
καὶ ἀγνοίᾳ πεπραγμένοις ὕστερον εἰς συναίσθησιν ἐλθὼν τῶν ἡμαρτημένων
αἰσχύνεται, ταῦτα καρπὸ ἂν εἴη ἄχρη το , ἄωρο εἰ βρῶ ιν καὶ εἰ οὐθὲν ἐπιτηδεῖο ·
καὶ γὰρ τέλος τῶν τοιούτων ἔργων οὐκ ἄλλο ἢ θάνατός ἐστιν, ὁ ἐχθρὸς Χριστῷ τῷ
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus. Some will take this to speak of others who lived to God but not in Christ Jesus. But we say perhaps it is not possible to live to God in Christ Jesus, since he saw Christ's day and rejoiced. For if Moses lived to God, he lived in Christ Jesus, and he esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt. Likewise, many prophets and righteous ones desired to see and hear what the apostles saw and heard, yet did not come into such longing and desire, missing the life in Christ Jesus to God. You may ask whether all who live to God in Christ Jesus must be dead to sin. One could reply: if someone once lived under sin, or if one enlightened by the Spirit searching the depths of God finds those who never lived under sin yet live to God in Christ Jesus, then it appears that whoever lives to God in Christ Jesus is already dead to sin; but if all sinned because Christ died for all, then it is evident that all who live in Christ Jesus once lived under sin and later became dead to it, thus living to God in Christ Jesus. Another might say it is possible that some are given to live to God in Christ Jesus without ever having been in sin, yet they are still dead to sin, just as sin was dead apart from the law, not arising from having once lived. But the divine apostle shows elsewhere the ease of victory: sin will not rule over you, for you are not under law but under grace. Consider the apostolic precision: how does ruling apply? To Christ he said death no longer rules; to us he said sin will not rule—neither was it fitting to say of Christ that sin does not rule, nor of us that death does not rule, lest the same be said of Christ and us as similar. After this, as giving cause that our sin does not rule, he says: you are not under law but under grace. For according to Paul, the power of sin is the law, and the law came in so that trespass might increase, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. Now we are under grace, not under law. For a righteous law does not lie in needing the letter's instruction to keep God's commandments, being taught by God, as Paul teaches concerning love: you need not write to one another, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another. If anyone has grown together with God's law so as not to wish the law otherwise than to be the human will, such a one is not under law but under grace. Thus we ought to think: in the Lord's law was his will. Just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to holiness. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. And since, as many have said (he says), we have kept watch, the name of righteousness is sometimes put in place of virtue; thus we say that now also this is what is said when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to virtue. And following the genitive of sin, the genitive of virtue is to be named righteousness in these things. Moreover, it will seem specifically that speaking of sanctification urges toward purity and bodily chastity for the one capable of receiving it. What fruit did you have then in the things you now are ashamed of? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit unto holiness, and the end is eternal life. By despising the fruit of slaves of sin as worthless talk, he says: for whatever someone formerly did in sin and ignorance, later coming to feel shame for the things committed, such fruit would be useless, unripe for food, and of no use. For the end of such works is nothing else but death, the enemy of Christ.
pass_b_english: Think of yourselves as having died to sin, yet made alive to God through Christ Jesus. Some may interpret this as referring to those who lived for God apart from Christ Jesus. But we suggest it might not be possible to truly live for God in Christ Jesus, since even Abraham saw Christ’s day and rejoiced. If Moses served God, he did so in communion with Christ, valuing the disgrace of Christ above Egypt’s treasures. Likewise, many prophets and righteous ones longed to witness what the apostles saw and heard, yet never attained that longing, missing the life in Christ Jesus before God. You may wonder whether all who live for God in Christ Jesus must be dead to sin. One response: if someone once lived under sin, or if one enlightened by the Spirit exploring God’s depths finds those who never lived under sin yet live for God in Christ Jesus, then it appears that whoever lives for God in Christ Jesus is already dead to sin. But if all sinned because Christ died for all, then it is clear that all who live in Christ Jesus once lived under sin and later became dead to it, thus living for God in Christ Jesus. Another might argue that some are enabled to live for God in Christ Jesus without ever having been in sin, yet they are still dead to sin, just as sin was powerless before the law, not arising from prior transgression. Yet the divine apostle affirms elsewhere the ease of victory: sin will not rule over you, for you are not under law but under grace. Consider the apostolic precision: how does ruling apply? To Christ he said death no longer rules; to us he said sin will not rule—nor would it be fitting to say of Christ that sin does not rule, nor of us that death does not rule, lest the same be said of Christ and us as similar. After this, as giving cause that our sin does not rule, he says: you are not under law but under grace. For according to Paul, the power of sin is the law, and the law came in so that trespass might increase, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. Now we are under grace, not under law. For a righteous law does not lie in needing the letter’s instruction to keep God’s commandments, being taught by God, as Paul teaches concerning love: you need not write to one another, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another. If anyone has grown together with God’s law so as not to wish the law otherwise than to be the human will, such a one is not under law but under grace. Thus we ought to think: in the Lord’s law was his will. Just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to holiness. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. And since, as many have said (he says), we have kept watch, the name of righteousness is sometimes put in place of virtue; thus we say that now also this is what is said when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to virtue. And following the genitive of sin, the genitive of virtue is to be named righteousness in these things. Moreover, it will seem specifically that speaking of sanctification urges toward purity and bodily chastity for the one capable of receiving it. What fruit did you have then in the things you now are ashamed of? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit unto holiness, and the end is eternal life. By despising the fruit of slaves of sin as worthless talk, he says: for whatever someone formerly did in sin and ignorance, later coming to feel shame for the things committed, such fruit would be useless, unripe for food, and of no use. For the end of such works is nothing else but death, the enemy of Christ.

Thus we must understand: the law of the Lord embodies his will. Once you offered your bodily members as servants to uncleanness and lawlessness, leading only to greater lawlessness; now offer them as servants to righteousness, leading to sanctification. When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. And since, as he notes, we have kept vigil, the term ‘righteousness’ is sometimes substituted for ‘virtue’; therefore, we say that even now, this is what is meant when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to virtue. Following the genitive of sin, the genitive of virtue is to be called righteousness in these contexts. Furthermore, it will clearly appear that speaking of sanctification calls for purity and moral integrity of life in those who are able to receive it. What gain did you reap then from the actions you now blush to recall? For the outcome of those actions is death. But now, having been liberated from sin and made servants of God, you possess the fruit that leads to holiness, and the final result is eternal life. By treating the fruit of sin’s slaves as meaningless chatter, he declares: whatever anyone once did in sin and ignorance, and later came to feel shame for those deeds, that fruit would be useless, unfit for consumption, and serving no purpose. For the end of such deeds is nothing other than death, the adversary of Christ.

bible_refs.note: Therefore, consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.
For sin will not have dominion over you, for you are not under law but under grace.

But now having been set free from sin and having become slaves of God, you have your fruit to sanctification and the end, eternal life. For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Core exhortation to reckon oneself dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.
Contrast: wages of sin is death, but gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus.
